dissections.title: Perigal: 3–4–5
dissections.citation: Henry Perigal, “On geometric dissections and transformations”, Messenger of Mathematics 2 (1873), pp. 103–106. Cuts through the centre of the square on the longer leg run parallel and perpendicular to the hypotenuse; the square on the shorter leg translates to the centre of the square on the hypotenuse. Exposition: Bill Casselman, “On the dissecting table”, Plus Magazine issue 16 (2001), https://plus.maths.org/content/dissecting-table. Two quadrilaterals turn by a half-turn and the others translate. This is a rigid-motion path, not a hinge.

dissections.title: Greek cross to square
dissections.citation: Henry Ernest Dudeney, Amusements in Mathematics (1917), Greek Cross Puzzles. The side of the square is the distance from an outer corner of one arm to an outer corner of the next, and the square stays at that angle while it slides. Gutenberg eBook 16713, https://www.gutenberg.org/files/16713/16713-h/16713-h.htm. The corner used here is the re-entrant point (1/2, 1/2) and one side is the vector (2, 1), so the side is sqrt(5). The four pieces are the intersections of the cross with the lattice of that square; they are unequal, which this solution allows.

dissections.title: 9×4 rectangle to square
dissections.citation: Henry Ernest Dudeney, Amusements in Mathematics (1917), solution 153, “A Cutting-Out Puzzle”: if the length-to-breadth ratio is greater than 1 and at most 4, and the rectangle is not an n-by-n tiling of the square, three pieces suffice. Gutenberg eBook 16713, https://www.gutenberg.org/files/16713/16713-h/16713-h.htm. The 9 by 4 rectangle has ratio 9/4, which is in that range, and the square has side 6. This is the parallel-cut case of that solution: one cut at x = 6 and one cut of the remaining 3 by 4 rectangle at y = 2.
